expectedSummary: Playful, sociable individuals of this Maltese–Yorkshire Terrier cross have trained for therapy work. In South Africa, Dr Suné Scholtz’s dog Morkie joined children’s play-therapy sessions, responding to hand signals and voice commands. In Indiana, Rocky completed a Love on a Leash evaluation and ten supervised visits, with his handler describing a friendly dog comfortable with adults and children.
expectedShortDescription: Selected Maltese–Yorkshire Terrier crosses have trained as therapy dogs for children’s sessions and library visits.

set.summary: The Morkie brings Maltese and Yorkshire Terrier ancestry together in a small companion cross. The name includes direct first crosses, litters from two Morkies and matings back to either parent breed. Those different breeding routes mean a Morkie is not necessarily an even first-generation mix; individual appearance and character remain variable.
set.shortDescription: A Maltese–Yorkshire Terrier companion cross that includes first crosses, later generations and backcrosses.
set.historicalRoots: Maltese–Yorkshire Terrier companion cross encompassing first-generation, intercross and backcross breeding.

appendSources.title: Sue Sue’s Precious Puppies — Morkie breeding definition
appendSources.evidence: Fresh entire substantive page independently read 2026-10-06: explicitly first Maltese/Yorkshire cross, backcross to either parent, or two Morkies together. Used only for identity and breeding routes; blanket friendly temperament excluded. Retained primary therapy accounts establish individual examples, not cross temperament.

rationale: Reopen prior hold: specific generation/parental-balance distinction makes useful concise identity copy without individual therapy achievements or inherited temperament. Appearance/character variability is a conservative scope statement, not a new predicted trait.

expectedSummary: Friendly and a joy to have around in his keeper’s account, sixteen-month-old Bug was a Poochon, a Bichon Frise–Poodle cross. Ten-year-old Pete’s owner described a loving dog who could be calm or joyfully playful. Pete rang sleigh bells on a doorknob to ask to go outside and used three barks to announce visitors.
expectedShortDescription: Poochon keepers describe Bug’s friendliness and Pete’s playful affection, bell signal for going outside and visitor barks.

set.summary: Poochons pair a Bichon Frise with Toy or Miniature Poodle ancestry. Breeding approaches differ: Rolling Meadows describes producing first crosses only, while other breeders include Poochon-to-Poochon matings and backcrosses to a parent breed. The same name therefore covers several generations, rather than one fixed parental balance or temperament.
set.shortDescription: A Bichon Frise–Poodle cross spanning Toy and Miniature ancestry, first crosses, later matings and backcrosses.
set.historicalRoots: Bichon Frise–Toy or Miniature Poodle cross, with first-cross and later-generation breeding approaches.

appendSources.title: Sue Sue’s Precious Puppies — Poochon generations
appendSources.evidence: Fresh entire substantive page independently read 2026-10-06. Specifies BichonFrise with Toy/MiniaturePoodle; F1 from two original parents, F2 two Poochons and F1B return to original parent. Used for generation definitions only.

appendSources.title: Rolling Meadows — first-person Poochon breeding approach
appendSources.evidence: Fresh actual substantive breeding sections read 2026-10-06, lines189–195 and285–290. Breeder explicitly says it produces first crosses and does not breed multigeneration dogs. This is its own practice, not universal Poochon norm. Inherited intelligence, health superiority, hypoallergenic, child suitability and uniform behavior assertions excluded.

rationale: Reopen prior hold: newly read primary program practices supply a meaningful cross/generation distinction. Bug/Pete behavior is removed, while those originals remain provenance.

expectedSummary: Energetic and affectionate in her keeper’s account, Peggy was a Shih-Poo at one year and nine months old. Her mother was a Shih Tzu and her father a Toy Poodle. Three-year-old Maggie’s owner described an intelligent dog who could be shy with unfamiliar people and noticed visitors entering the home. Regular grooming was part of Maggie’s routine.
expectedShortDescription: Shih-Poo owners describe Peggy’s energy and affection, and Maggie’s shyness with unfamiliar people and alertness to visitors.

set.summary: The Shih-Poo combines Shih Tzu and Poodle ancestry, with more than one breeding route behind the name. StonyRidge describes first crosses using Toy Poodles, while a separately documented breeding dog has a Toy Poodle father and a first-cross Shih-Poo mother. These are different generations of the cross, so the label alone does not fix a dog’s proportions, coat or character.
set.shortDescription: A Shih Tzu–Poodle cross found in both first-generation litters and Poodle backcrosses, with individual variation.
set.historicalRoots: Shih Tzu–Poodle cross documented in first-generation Toy-Poodle matings and later Poodle backcrosses.

Only actual stated mating practice adopted; inherited character, hypoallergenic, medical benefits and guarantee claims excluded.

Header says Poodle because site lacked Shih-Poo choice; keeper explicitly corrects it: F1B Shih-Poo, ToyPoodle father and F1Shih-Poo mother. Used only as direct documented existence of this backcross, not population character, pedigree certification, standardized dimensions or health claims.

rationale: Reopen prior hold: original mating declarations establish distinct first-cross/backcross scope, without transferring Peggy/Maggie or Sterling personality to the type.

expectedSummary: Rascal’s keeper described a vigilant but loving four-year-old who obeyed commands and chased trespassing varmints. Another owner reported that five-year-old Capone knew more than 50 verbal commands and 20 signs. American Bandogge accounts cover varied crosses: Rascal’s father was a Great Dane and his mother a Pit Bull–Neapolitan Mastiff cross, while Capone was an English Mastiff–Pit Bull cross.
expectedShortDescription: Named Bandogges include vigilant, affectionate Rascal and Capone, whose owner reported a large verbal and sign vocabulary.

set.summary: Modern dogs called American Bandogges have varied ancestry: documented crosses include English Mastiff–Pit Bull and combinations involving Great Dane and Neapolitan Mastiff. Some programs select dogs for guarding and hog-catching work; American Sentinel dates its own breeding to 2000. These working aims and line histories do not define one fixed cross or predict an individual dog’s behavior.
set.shortDescription: A name used for varied modern working lines and mastiff–bull-type crosses, with differing ancestry and selection aims.
set.historicalRoots: Modern varied working lines and crosses; American Sentinel records its own guard/catch breeding program from2000.

appendSources.title: American Sentinel K9 — own modern program origins and roles
appendSources.evidence: Fresh substantive home page independently read 2026-10-06. Program records beginning2000 and selection for guardian/hog-catch roles. Used only as own modern breeding history and intended work. Oldest/best/guaranteed performance or family-safety assertions not adopted.

appendSources.title: American Sentinel K9 — scope of the Bandogge name
appendSources.evidence: Fresh substantive article independently read 2026-10-06. Author explicitly calls AmericanSentinel one of many bandog types and rejects a universal fixed-parentage definition. His polemical ancient etymology, claims about other breeders and combative ability are not adopted as facts or endorsements. Retained original Rascal/Capone accounts separately establish actual differing reported modern ancestry.

rationale: Reopen prior hold: combine actual heterogeneous parentage with a distinctly identified working program’s own history. Do not equate every Bandogge with American Sentinel or project individual behavior.

expectedSummary: Friendly, active and playful in his rescue’s account, Chesador Prancer had arrived with his brother Blitzen after jumping a five- to six-foot chain-link fence at their previous home. Beagles and Buddies reported that the brothers had stayed inside its fences. Its profile identified four-year-old Prancer as a Labrador Retriever–Chesapeake Bay Retriever cross.
expectedShortDescription: Beagles and Buddies described Chesador Prancer as playful and active, with a history of jumping his former home’s fence.

set.summary: The Chesador is a Labrador Retriever–Chesapeake Bay Retriever cross. The name appears in a breeder’s 2011 account of a brown litter in Minnesota; a Michigan program later described its own black puppies with rippled coats. These records show variation within the named cross, rather than a single required color or a predictable temperament.
set.shortDescription: A Labrador–Chesapeake Bay Retriever cross, documented in brown and black litters with variation in coat.
set.historicalRoots: Documented Labrador Retriever–Chesapeake Bay Retriever cross; named breeding records include a Minnesota litter in2011.

expectedSummary: Companionship and water are favorites of Harry, a ten-year-old Sprocker whom Malcata Animal Association described enjoying walks, swims and sofa evenings. This Springer–Cocker Spaniel cross appears in Liza Leonard’s firsthand account of Patch and Rufus: Patch approached for attention, while Rufus was initially shy; both liked balls and running.

set.summary: A spaniel cross used in British shooting, the Sprocker combines English Springer and Cocker ancestry. Gundog writer David Tomlinson describes both first crosses and later Sprocker matings, with wide variation in size and coat colour rather than one fixed appearance. A working pedigree does not make temperament predictable; even his own dog’s biddability is presented as luck rather than a general promise.
set.shortDescription: A Springer–Cocker cross used in shooting, with variable size and coat; a working pedigree is no temperament guarantee.

appendSources.title: David Tomlinson / Shooting UK — What is a sprocker?
appendSources.evidence: Fresh full primary firsthand article read2026-10-06. Working-stock enthusiasm is a qualified observation; own Emma’s unusual biddability explicitly attributed to luck rather than breeding. Copy retains concrete identity/working context and variation, not medical hybrid-vigour claims, registry dates or guaranteed ability.

decisionRationale: A useful exact-type account is feasible from parentage, working context, directly observed variation and narrowly attributed experience; no registry recognition or uniform type temperament required. Remove editorial evidence hold after lead independently reviews and applies correction.
newDiscovery: Follow-up to parent reminder that feasible bounded rewrites must precede evidence holds.

expectedSummary: Lively and affectionate in one rescue’s firsthand observations, the Springador is a Labrador–Springer Spaniel cross with documented working roles. Molly, an adult in foster care, is described as clever and communicative, with a chase instinct and a need for close company. Kenya Customs’ Cooper belongs to a trained patrol team detecting narcotics and explosives across borders.

set.summary: A Labrador–English Springer Spaniel cross found as both a companion and a hunting dog in Britain. Trainer Pippa Mattinson reports friendly, outgoing Springadors in her experience, while stressing that behaviour and mature size vary. The name describes parentage rather than a uniform temperament; littermates can differ in size, and working instincts are not reliably predicted by the cross alone.
set.shortDescription: A Labrador–Springer cross found in British homes and hunting, with variable size, character and working drive.
